title: Steady-state flush latency sensitivity log
content:
Purpose:
This note captures a focused set of steady-state experiments that probe how the flush decision (time-based vs size-based vs hybrid) affects tail latency and fairness under realistic long-running workloads. Goal: produce actionable guardrails for the default flush policy and a short list of mitigations when customers see p95/p99 spikes during steady traffic bursts.

Background and motivation:
We observed intermittent p99 spikes on long-lived GPU workers serving mixed traffic (short chat + long-completion). Prior probes pointed to batch formation hysteresis and rare coalescence delays. Instead of only testing cold-start bursts, I ran sustained 30–60 minute steady-state runs to expose oscillation behavior (batch growth/flush cycles) and how KV cache pressure interacts with flush timing.

Experiment setup (hardware + software):
- Cluster: 8x A100-40GB workers (prod-ish), isolated run, controlled driver node.
- Serving runtime: local dev build at commit 2a9b3f7 (trace-enabled, debug logging on batch controller).
- Model: opt-6.7b-quant (serving path used by Hosted QA), avg token gen time ~1.8ms/token, kv-cache enabled.
- Traffic generator: custom client harness (steady-mixer) that emits mixed client profiles: 60% short (prompt len 40, gen len 20), 30% medium (prompt 160, gen 80), 10% long (prompt 400, gen 200). Inter-arrival adheres to poisson with lambda tuned to produce 1800 rps aggregate on single node.
- Measurements: request and token latencies logged, batch sizes, flush triggers (timeout vs size), queue-occupancy time series (1s buckets), GPU util, KV cache hit-rate, and scheduler trace ids for correlation.
- Sweep parameters:
  * timeout_ms: [1, 3, 6, 12, 25] (time-based flush)
  * max_batch: [8, 16, 32, 64] (size cap)
  * hybrid_policy: size-first (flush when size reached or timeout), timeout-first (flush on timeout unless min-size), and soft-grace (allow +20% over max for 2ms to try coalesce).

Key metrics collected:
- p50/p95/p99 request latency (end-to-end): includes queue/wait + service time
- service time (generation only) and queue wait separately
- batch formation time (time between first arrival and flush)
- starvation events (batches flushed with size <= 2 for > 30s)
- fairness index: median queue wait per client cohort (short/medium/long) normalized
- throughput (tokens/s and requests/s) and GPU util

High-level observations (summary):
1) Very small timeouts (<=3ms) keep p50 low but increase p99 for long completions. We think short-timeout causes excessive flushing leading to smaller batches and more variance in tail due to head-of-line effects when a long request is served alone.
2) Large timeouts (>=12ms) improve throughput and reduce average cost per token but can create bursty queue growth that, when combined with heterogeneous lengths, forces the controller to flush very large batches sporadically — these correlate with p99 spikes because a large batch containing many long requests leads to longer service times that push other requests' tails out.
3) Hybrid policies that prioritized size over timeout tended to improve aggregate throughput but skewed fairness against short requests: short requests waited disproportionately longer to reach a large batch. Conversely, timeout-first policies favored short requests but raised cost.
4) Soft-grace policies (allow a small overshoot) reduced p99 by ~8–12% vs strict max_batch in a majority of runs — small additional wait allowed effective coalescence of short requests without worsening fairness much.

Representative numbers (steady run averages across 30m):
- timeout_ms=3, max_batch=16, policy=timeout-first:
  p50=14ms, p95=72ms, p99=215ms, avg batch size=6.1, GPU util=68%, tokens/s=44k
- timeout_ms=12, max_batch=64, policy=size-first:
  p50=22ms, p95=85ms, p99=560ms (occasional big-batch), avg batch size=23.4, GPU util=84%, tokens/s=58k
- timeout_ms=6, max_batch=32, policy=soft-grace (+20% for 2ms):
  p50=18ms, p95=68ms, p99=195ms, avg batch size=14.9, GPU util=78%, tokens/s=51k

Profiling snippets and hypotheses:
- Trace correlation: p99 events align with two patterns: (A) a large batch containing multiple long requests triggers long service time; (B) KV cache eviction thrash when many long sequences cause KV churn — this increases per-token generation time and amplifies tail.
- CPU-side activity: batch controller spent short bursts (~10–30ms every ~5s) in O(n) reordering work when applying fairness demotion heuristics. These micro-pauses coincide with a slight increase in queue latency for short requests.
- Memory/KV: when avg batch size > 20 with long requests, observed a 12% drop in KV cache hit rate and 1.3x increase in gen-time per token for affected traces.

Fairness deep-dive (short vs long cohorts):
- With size-first policies, short cohort median wait rose from 8ms -> 26ms as max_batch increased. Worst-case short request wait reached 180ms in runs where a long request arrived early in a forming batch.
- Timeout-first prioritized short requests and produced lower median for short cohort but increased global p99 because many medium/long requests could be flushed alone.
- Soft-grace finds middle ground: short median wait 12–16ms, long cohort p99 reduced vs timeout-first.

Edge-case behavior noticed:
- Oscillation: with timeout set around 6ms and max_batch 32 we observed a repeating pattern where queue occupancy slowly climbs then flushes, then drops, repeating every ~400–700ms. This led to compound p99 amplification periodically (not steady but cyclical).
- Preemption interplay: preemption on very large batches (evicting low-priority requests to form smaller batches) reduces p99 but increases scheduler CPU overhead.

Recommendations (short):
1) Default policy for Hosted should be soft-grace hybrid: timeout_ms=6ms, max_batch=32, overshoot 15–25% for 1–3ms. Rationale: good balance of p50/p95 and improved p99 in steady mixed workloads.
2) Add telemetry flags: expose avg batch size, overshoot count, and observed KV-hit ratio to Console for live troubleshooting.
3) Implement an adaptive fallback: if a worker sees repeating oscillation signature (periodic large flush cycles), temporarily reduce max_batch by 25% and increase timeout by 2ms for 10s window to break the cycle.
4) Micro-optimization: move fairness demotion work off the critical path (defer to timer or worker thread) to avoid short CPU-induced queue pauses.

Next steps / experiments to validate:
- Run same steady-state mix on cheaper/denser hardware (H100-80GB and lower memory variants) to quantify KV-pressure correlation with memory.
- Test with real customer traces (ENG-1342) to validate whether synthetic mix covers pathologies.
- A/B test soft-grace default on a small Hosted roll to capture production telemetry for one week.

Troubleshooting checklist (for SREs/customer-facing support):
- If customer reports p99 spikes: check batch-size histogram for the worker, KV-hit rate, and overshoot_count.
- If oscillation pattern seen: trigger mitigation toggles (reduce max_batch, enable transient small-timeout), collect trace ids around spike window, escalate if p99 > 500ms repeatedly.

Raw excerpts (log examples):
- Trace 2024-12-04T13:22:18Z (p99 spike)
  batch_id=bb-28421 size=45 flush=soft-grace overshoot=9 queued=0 reason=timeout
  cohort_counts=(short:18, medium:17, long:10) swarm_gen_time=2.3ms/token kv_hit=0.72

- Controller debug: "demote: scanned=240, demoted=6, cpu-ms=11"

Open questions / unresolved:
- What is the best signal to detect KV-thrashing early? Per-batch kv-hit is noisy; should we surface an exponentially smoothed kv-hit metric?
- How aggressive should preemption be before it becomes counterproductive from a CPU overhead perspective?
- Are there model-specific knobs (e.g., kv-chunk-size) we should expose to reduce per-token sensitivity when long sequences dominate?

Appendix: commands and data collection notes:
- Start harness: python tools/steady_mixer.py --rps 1800 --mix short:60,med:30,long:10 --seed 42 --duration 1800
- Enable tracing: export SRV_TRACE=1; ./bin/serving-runtime --batch-debug=1 --trace-sample-rate=0.1
- Collect metrics: prometheus scrape interval 5s, use grafana panel "batching/formation" for live view

Conclusions:
Steady-state behavior reveals that small config tweaks (a few ms and a small overshoot allowance) materially change tail characteristics. The soft-grace hybrid plus a lightweight oscillation detector seems a promising default for balancing cost, throughput, and p99. Need to validate with production traces and a short canary rollout.

Notes to self: upload selected traces to S3 (s3://redwood-bench/flush-experiments/2024-11-07/) and tag ENG-1342 for review. Follow up with Lina on adaptive fallback prototype next week.
